# FDS Error Code Explorer

> What every Famicom Disk System error code means, in plain language: what triggers it, what the screen shows, and where the fault actually lives.

Source: https://stephen-arsenault.github.io/fds-error-explorer/

Behaviour is traced from static analysis of one 8 KB Famicom Disk System
BIOS image (`disksys.rom`), mapped at $E000; nothing was executed or
emulated. Physical details of the media and drive come from the NESdev
Wiki and community hardware documentation.

Codes $0A-$0F, $35 and $40 appear in circulating tables but have no raise
site in this ROM and cannot occur. $35 is not an error: it is the
warm-boot signature written to $0102.

## Categories

- **Drive & power** (3 codes) — the hardware, before any data is read
- **Wrong disk** (7 codes) — the disk is readable, but it isn't the one asked for
- **Unreadable data** (7 codes) — the right disk, but the bytes came back wrong
- **Saving failed** (3 codes) — only ever raised while writing to the disk
- **Software rule** (2 codes) — nothing physical is wrong; a check in software said no

## Codes

### ERR.01 — The drive doesn't think there's a disk in it

- Category: Drive & power
- When: at start-up and during play
- On screen: DISK SET / ERR.01

The drive says there is nothing in it. It never looks at the disk — it feels for a small switch that a disk presses when pushed all the way in.

So a disk that is not fully seated, or a worn switch, looks the same as an empty slot. That is why you can be looking straight at a disk and still get this.

**What triggers it.** Checked when the drive starts up, and again after every chunk of data it reads. Taking the disk out mid-load gives the same result as never inserting one.

**Worth knowing.**

- Push the disk firmly all the way in. That is usually all it takes.
- The system cannot tell 'no disk' apart from 'disk in, switch not pressed'.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E678 DriveReadyWait · $E42A SetupWriteParams · $E757 WriteBlockEnd condition: $4032 bit 0 set Carry gate at $E77C from DriveReadyWait and WriteBlockEnd; return-address discard at $E43E from the API prologue.

### ERR.02 — The drive isn't receiving proper power

- Category: Drive & power
- When: at start-up and during play
- On screen: BATTERY / ERR.02

The drive is not getting the power it needs. This is tested before the disk is touched at all.

BATTERY on screen is too specific. The unit runs from batteries or a mains adapter and this appears either way, so read it as 'power'.

**What triggers it.** The system sends a signal to the drive and listens for it coming back. Anything breaking that path counts: a dead adapter, flat batteries, corroded contacts, dirty connectors.

**Worth knowing.**

- Nothing to do with the disk — this happens before the disk is read.
- Also appears when power is present but not reaching the drive properly.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E669 DriveReadyWait condition: write $F9|$80 → $4026, then EOR $4033, test bit 7 Carry gate at $E77C.

### ERR.03 — Something tried to save to a protected disk

- Category: Drive & power
- When: only from a running game
- On screen: ERR.03 with no message line

A game tried to save, and the disk is set to refuse writes. Nothing was written and nothing was harmed.

To check: hold the disk as it goes into the drive and look at the top-left corner of the side facing in. A small tab there means writing is allowed. A gap where it used to be means protected.

**What triggers it.** Only checked when saving. Loading ignores it, so a protected disk plays normally and fails the moment a game tries to save.

**Worth knowing.**

- Hole open = protected. Cover it with tape to allow writing again; the tab does not go back on.
- The drive feels for the tab with a small lever, which can stick when dirty and report protection on a perfectly good disk.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E435 SetupWriteParams condition: $4032 bit 2 set (Protect flag) Reached only when the read/write flag is clear; $E433 BCS skips it for reads. Per the NESdev Wiki the same flag reads 1 for a broken tab or an ejected disk.

### ERR.04 — The disk was published by someone other than the game expected

- Category: Wrong disk
- When: only from a running game
- On screen: ERR.04 with no message line

The disk was made by a different publisher than the game asked for.

In practice: a game asked you to swap disks and got something unrelated.

**What triggers it.** A game can name the disk it expects before loading from it. The system compares what is written on the disk against that and stops at the first thing that does not match.

**Worth knowing.**

- Games choose which details to check, so many never produce this at all.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E445 CheckDiskHeader, byte 0 (header offset $0F) condition: disk byte ≠ caller template byte, and template byte ≠ $FF Code comes from the running counter in $08, initialised to 4. Boot template at $EFF5 is FF FF FF FF FF FF 00 00 FF FF.

### ERR.05 — This disk belongs to a different game

- Category: Wrong disk
- When: only from a running game
- On screen: ERR.05 with no message line

The disk belongs to a different game than the one running. You have inserted a disk from another title.

**What triggers it.** A game can name the disk it expects. This covers the short name and type written on the disk, and any part of it not matching gives this same number.

**Worth knowing.**

- It cannot tell you which part did not match.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E445 CheckDiskHeader, bytes 1–4 (header offsets $10–$13) condition: disk byte ≠ caller template byte, and template byte ≠ $FF The counter increment at $E46D is suppressed for these four positions.

### ERR.06 — The disk is a different revision of the game

- Category: Wrong disk
- When: only from a running game
- On screen: ERR.06 with no message line

Same game, different edition. The running game expects its own version and this disk is another.

Uncommon: it needs a game that was printed twice, and that bothers to check.

**What triggers it.** Disks record a version number, and the running game asked for a particular one.

**Worth knowing.**

- Most games do not check this.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E445 CheckDiskHeader, byte 5 (header offset $14) condition: disk byte ≠ caller template byte, and template byte ≠ $FF Boot template byte 5 at $EFF5 is $FF.

### ERR.07 — The disk is in the wrong way round — flip it

- Category: Wrong disk
- When: at start-up and during play
- On screen: A·B SIDE / ERR.07

The disk is in the wrong way round. Each side holds different data, so a side works like its own disk.

Take it out, turn it over, put it back. Starting the system with the B side facing in gives this too.

**What triggers it.** Disks record which side is which. The system, or the game you are playing, wanted the other one.

**Worth knowing.**

- If a game asks you to flip and you put the same side back in, you will see this again.
- One of only four errors that names the problem on screen instead of showing a bare number.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E445 CheckDiskHeader, byte 6 (header offset $15) condition: disk byte ≠ caller template byte, and template byte ≠ $FF Message string 'A.B SIDE' at $F02E+16. Boot template byte 6 at $EFF5 is $00, not a wildcard.

### ERR.08 — Wrong disk in a multi-disk set

- Category: Wrong disk
- When: at start-up and during play
- On screen: DISK NO. / ERR.08

Bigger games came on more than one disk. The game asked for a particular one and this is not it.

Insert the disk it asked for. Starting the system with anything but the first disk of a set gives this too.

**What triggers it.** Disks record their number within a set, and it is compared against the one wanted.

**Worth knowing.**

- The number on the label is the one the game means.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E445 CheckDiskHeader, byte 7 (header offset $16) condition: disk byte ≠ caller template byte, and template byte ≠ $FF Message string 'DISK NO.' at $F02E+24. Boot template byte 7 at $EFF5 is $00, not a wildcard.

### ERR.09 — This is the wrong kind of disk

- Category: Wrong disk
- When: only from a running game
- On screen: ERR.09 with no message line

There were two kinds: ordinary yellow disks, and blue ones. A game wanted one kind and got the other.

Blue disks have a sliding cover over the opening and no small tab along the top edge, so they are easy to tell apart by eye.

**What triggers it.** Blue disks were made for Nintendo's national high-score contests — you carried them to a kiosk that read your score off the disk. Only those games check this, which is why it is so rarely seen.

**Worth knowing.**

- Both kinds are perfectly good disks. This is not damage.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E445 CheckDiskHeader, byte 8 (header offset $17) condition: disk byte ≠ caller template byte, and template byte ≠ $FF Documented as 'disk type (FMC)': $01 for FMC blue-disk releases, $00 otherwise.

### ERR.10 — An unidentified detail on the disk does not match

- Category: Wrong disk
- When: only from a running game
- On screen: ERR.10 with no message line

One of the details written on the disk is not what the game expected — and it is the one detail nobody has worked out the purpose of.

It reads as zero on every commercial game anyone has examined.

**What triggers it.** It would take a game deliberately demanding something unusual here, which no known release does. In practice it points to a homemade or altered disk.

**Worth knowing.**

- Very rarely seen.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E445 CheckDiskHeader, byte 9 (header offset $18) condition: disk byte ≠ caller template byte, and template byte ≠ $FF Documented as unknown, $00 in all known games. $E45B rewrites the counter value $0A to $10 before the gate.

### ERR.20 — The game loaded fine but didn't show the required Nintendo screen

- Category: Software rule
- When: start-up only
- On screen: DISK TROUBLE / ERR.20

Nothing is wrong with the disk. It loaded perfectly and the game is already in memory.

Before starting a game, the system checks that the game has drawn Nintendo's copyright notice on screen. If it has not, the system refuses to run it.

**What triggers it.** It compares what the game has put on screen against a copy held inside the console. One character out of place is enough. Unlicensed disks that skipped the notice stop here.

**Worth knowing.**

- The screen still reads DISK TROUBLE, which is misleading — the disk is fine.

**In the ROM.** raise site $EF6A RESET (raised) → $F431 CopyrightCheck (decided) condition: video memory $2800–$28DF ≠ tile table at $ED37 $ED37 spells 'NINTENDO' and 'FAMILY CO…' in the BIOS tile encoding.

### ERR.21 — This does not look like a Famicom disk

- Category: Unreadable data
- When: at start-up and during play
- On screen: DISK TROUBLE / ERR.21

Every genuine Famicom disk begins with the same fourteen-character marking. This one does not carry it.

Either it is not a Famicom disk, or the very beginning of it is too damaged to read.

**What triggers it.** The system reads those first fourteen characters and compares them one at a time against a copy held inside the console.

**Worth knowing.**

- What you would expect from a blank disk, a badly worn one, or a disk from another system.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E6FA ReadVerifyDiskInfo condition: disk byte ≠ table byte at $E6D5+Y, for Y = $0D down to 0 The table stores '*NINTENDO-HVC*' reversed, because the loop counts down while the disk streams forward.

### ERR.22 — The part of the disk that names the game is missing

- Category: Unreadable data
- When: at start-up and during play
- On screen: DISK TROUBLE / ERR.22

A disk stores its data as a run of labelled sections, read in a fixed order. The first should be the one naming the game, and it is not.

Since this is the very first thing read, it usually means the disk is unreadable from the start rather than damaged partway through.

**What triggers it.** The system checks each section's label before reading it, and this one was not what should come first.

**Worth knowing.**

- ERR.22 to ERR.25 are the same check at four points in the sequence.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E697 ReadBlockType condition: tag byte read ≠ expected block type Code = block type + $21 via CLC / ADC #$21.

### ERR.23 — The list of files on the disk is missing

- Category: Unreadable data
- When: at start-up and during play
- On screen: DISK TROUBLE / ERR.23

After naming the game, a disk says how many files it holds. That part is not where it should be.

The disk named itself correctly, so it is the right disk and it is readable. The data stops making sense immediately after that.

**What triggers it.** Data is stored as labelled sections read in a fixed order, and this section's label was not what should come next.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E697 ReadBlockType condition: tag byte read ≠ expected block type Code = block type + $21.

### ERR.24 — A file's label is missing

- Category: Unreadable data
- When: at start-up and during play
- On screen: DISK TROUBLE / ERR.24

Each file on the disk starts with a short label describing it. The system expected one and found something else.

Everything before this read correctly, so it usually means damage partway through the disk.

**What triggers it.** Files are stored as a label followed by the contents, and the label that should have come next was not there.

**Worth knowing.**

- The label and the contents are stored separately, which is why a missing label and missing contents are different numbers.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E697 ReadBlockType condition: tag byte read ≠ expected block type Code = block type + $21.

### ERR.25 — A file's contents are missing

- Category: Unreadable data
- When: at start-up and during play
- On screen: DISK TROUBLE / ERR.25

A file's label read fine, so the system knows a file is coming and how big it should be. The contents that should follow are not there.

This is the furthest into a disk the related errors reach — everything up to this point read correctly.

**What triggers it.** Files are stored as a label followed by the contents. The two have become separated.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E697 ReadBlockType condition: tag byte read ≠ expected block type Code = block type + $21.

### ERR.26 — A save did not record properly

- Category: Saving failed
- When: only from a running game
- On screen: DISK TROUBLE / ERR.26

The system reads back everything it writes and compares the two. They did not match, so the save cannot be trusted.

Usually a worn disk surface, or a drive that has drifted out of alignment.

**What triggers it.** Every save is checked by reading it straight back. A single byte out of place stops the operation.

**Worth knowing.**

- It cannot tell you which part of the save failed.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E5C0 · $E5D2 · $E5FC · $E62B, all in WriteVerifyBlock condition: byte read back ≠ byte written All four go through the zero gate at $E77F.

### ERR.27 — Part of the disk read back damaged

- Category: Unreadable data
- When: at start-up and during play
- On screen: DISK TROUBLE / ERR.27

The system checks its own arithmetic on every chunk of data it loads, and on this one the numbers did not agree. At least one byte came back wrong.

This is the usual sign of a worn, scratched or dirty disk, and the most common reason an old disk stops loading.

**What triggers it.** Checked after every chunk. The system tries twice before reporting it, so the damage is consistent rather than a passing glitch.

**Worth knowing.**

- Cleaning the disk is worth trying. Beyond that, the data itself has degraded.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E71E CheckBlockEnd condition: $4030 bit 4 set after arming CRC control Reached by a raw branch to $E781, bypassing both throw gates.

### ERR.28 — Data stopped sooner than expected

- Category: Unreadable data
- When: at start-up and during play
- On screen: DISK TROUBLE / ERR.28

A chunk of data ended while the system was still expecting more of it — there is less on the disk than the disk itself claimed.

Usually damage, or the drive losing its place partway through.

**What triggers it.** The system watches for an end marker while reading, and saw it before it had read everything it was told to expect.

**Worth knowing.**

- Different from ERR.27: this is data that is too short, that is data that is wrong.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E709 CheckBlockEnd · $E766 ReadBlockToRAM condition: $4030 bit 6 set while bytes remain Both sites branch raw to $E781.

### ERR.29 — The disk ran out of room while saving

- Category: Saving failed
- When: only from a running game
- On screen: DISK TROUBLE / ERR.29

A save stopped partway because there was no more space to write into.

**What triggers it.** The drive signalled the end of the writable area before the system had finished writing.

**Worth knowing.**

- The save is incomplete and the disk is left partly written.
- ERR.28 is this same thing happening while loading.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E72C WriteBlockEnd condition: $4030 bit 6 set during a write Raw branch to $E781.

### ERR.30 — The drive stopped being ready during a save

- Category: Saving failed
- When: only from a running game
- On screen: ERR.30 with no message line

The drive stopped being ready partway through a save, so the save did not finish.

**What triggers it.** After writing, the system pauses briefly and then asks the drive whether it is still ready. It was not.

**Worth knowing.**

- The pause is a fixed length rather than a measured one, so a marginal drive may pass or fail it inconsistently.
- The screen shows only the number, with no message above it.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E743 WriteBlockEnd condition: $4032 bit 1 set after a busy wait of ~178 iterations Raw branch to $E781.

### ERR.31 — A program asked for more files than the disk holds

- Category: Software rule
- When: only from a running game
- On screen: ERR.31 with no message line

A game asked for more files than the disk holds. Nothing is broken — the request was impossible.

**What triggers it.** The system counts what is on the disk and compares it against what was asked for.

**Worth knowing.**

- Nothing is interrupted: the drive keeps running and the game simply gets a refusal back.
- The screen shows only the number, with no message above it.

**In the ROM.** raise site $E2DE AdjustFileCount condition: requested count > count present on disk Returned via TXA / RTS at $E2F5, never through the throw block at $E778.
